source_text: Tam enim scelestum est, quod suscepit praevaricatio pudenda Babylonis, ut cum a nobis obicitur, a vobis negetur; et tam sanctum est, quod a nobis creditur, ut sub umbra eius delitescere, licet adversaria mente, cupiatis. Nam cum ego quidquid disputationis vestrae sparsim membris tenebatur exprimerem, et summam quaestionis in brevitatem cogerem, ut ecclesiasticae dissensionis causa, quanta et qualis esset, sine fumo et nebulis proderetur, dixi liberum a vobis arbitrium negari, et Deum nascentium conditorem; porro a nobis id utrumque defendi, et ob hoc vos imperitis auribus de nominibus catholicorum virorum, qui propter fidem apostolicam quam tuemur, nobiscum laborant, ciere inanem fragorem, ut qui timuissent Caelestiani a vobis dici, amitterent caelestis fidei dignitatem; et qui expavissent ne a vobis Pelagiani dicerentur, in Manichaeorum pelagus praecipitarentur; putarentque se imperiti quique non posse Christianos appellari, si eos Traduciani Pelagianos vocassent; cum e regione prudentes statuerent, quamvis nominum invidiam sibi et iniuriam sustinendam magis, quam fidem catholicam relinquendam. Sed ne vel hoc ipsum convicii genus vestro inventum ingenio glorieris; recordamini, ab omnibus quidem haereticis diversa nos vocabula solere suscipere; sed in Synodo Ariminensi vehementius claruisse, quid apud plumbeos animos vel ambiguitas verbi, vel comminatio novi vocabuli possit sceleris obtinere. Nam cum sub Ariano principe, vir magnae constantiae, fidei sanissimae, Athanasius Alexandrinus episcopus, dilapso a fide Apostolorum omni pene mundo, et impiatis temporibus obstitisset, atque ob hoc in exsilia coactus esset; de sescentis et quinquaginta, ut fertur, episcopis, vix septem inventi sunt, quibus cariora essent Dei praecepta quam regis; videlicet ut nec in Athanasii damnationem convenirent, nec Trinitatis confessionem negarent. Illa vero omnis deiectorum pectorum multitudo, extra iniuriarum metum, hac est potissimum vel nominis comminatione, ne Athanasiana vocaretur, vel interrogationis calliditate decepta.
pass_a_gloss: For so criminal is that which the shameful prevarication of Babylon has taken up, that when it is objected by us, it is denied by you; and so holy is that which is believed by us, that you desire to hide under its shadow, though with an adversary mind. For when I was expressing whatever of your disputation was being held scattered in members, and was compelling the sum of the question into brevity, that the cause of ecclesiastical dissension, how great and of what quality it was, might be brought forth without smoke and clouds, I said that free choice is denied by you, and God the founder of those being born; further that both are defended by us, and on account of this you stir an empty crash to unskilled ears from the names of catholic men, who on account of the apostolic faith which we guard labor with us, so that those who had feared to be called Caelestian by you would lose the dignity of heavenly faith; and those who had panicked lest they be called Pelagians by you would be thrown headlong into the sea of the Manichaeans; and the unskilled each would think they cannot be called Christians, if the Traduciani had called them Pelagians; when from the other side the prudent would establish that the ill-will of names is more to be sustained for themselves and the injury, than the catholic faith to be left. But lest you glory that even this kind of insult was invented by your talent; remember, that we are accustomed to take up diverse names from all heretics indeed; but in the Synod of Ariminum it shone more vehemently, what among leaden minds either the ambiguity of a word, or the threatening of a new name, can obtain of crime. For when under an Arian prince, a man of great constancy, of most sound faith, Athanasius the Alexandrian bishop, with almost the whole world having slipped from the faith of the Apostles, and with times made impious, had stood against, and on account of this had been forced into exiles; from six hundred and fifty, as it is said, bishops, scarcely seven were found, to whom the precepts of God were dearer than of the king; namely that they would neither come together into the condemnation of Athanasius, nor deny the confession of the Trinity. But that whole multitude of cast-down breasts, besides fear of injuries, was deceived most of all either by this threatening of a name, lest it be called Athanasian, or by the cunning of a question.

Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: What Babylon's shameful betrayal has undertaken is so wicked that, when we charge you with it, you deny it. What we believe is so holy that you wish to hide in its shade, though your minds oppose it. For when I drew out what was scattered throughout the parts of your argument and compressed the issue into a brief statement, so that the extent and character of the cause of the Church's division would appear without smoke or mist, I said that you deny both free choice and God as the Creator of newborn children, while we defend both. That is why you raise an empty din in uneducated ears about the names of catholic men who struggle alongside us for the apostolic faith we defend. Those afraid of being called Caelestians by you lose the dignity of heavenly faith; those terrified of being called Pelagians plunge into the sea of Manichaeism. Uneducated people come to think they cannot be called Christians if the advocates of inherited sin have called them Pelagians. Sensible people, by contrast, decide that they must endure any hatred or insult attached to names rather than abandon the catholic faith.

But do not boast that even this type of abuse was invented by your ingenuity. Remember that all heretics commonly give us different names. At the council of Rimini it became especially clear what wickedness an ambiguous word or the threat of a new label can achieve in leaden minds. Under an Arian ruler, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, a man of great steadfastness and thoroughly sound faith, resisted after almost the whole world had slipped away from the apostles' faith and the times had become impious. For this he was driven into exile. Out of six hundred and fifty bishops, as the report goes, scarcely seven were found who valued God's commands more than the king's: they would neither agree to Athanasius's condemnation nor deny the confession of the Trinity. Besides fear of mistreatment, the entire crowd of those broken spirits was deceived chiefly either by the threatening label “Athanasian” or by a cunning question.

choices.why: Julian's label for teachers of tradux peccati. Keep the polemic name as a description of transmitted sin, not as a theory of the soul's origin.
Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: Julian makes wordplays on Caelestian/heavenly and Pelagian/sea. The argument and historical claims are translated as he presents them, not independently endorsed.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
